title: Question 6
stem:
Two parallel vertical metal plates are connected to a power supply, as shown in Fig. 6.1.
{{figure:figure_6_1}}
Fig. 6.1
The separation of the plates is $16\text{ mm}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: On Fig. 6.1, draw at least six field lines to represent the electric field between the plates.

markscheme_points.text: at least six horizontal lines equally spaced and arrow to the right

hints: Hint 1: Look at the + and - terminals at the bottom of Fig. 6.1 to work out which plate is positive, and recall what the field looks like when it is uniform between two parallel plates.
parts.proper_answer: Draw at least six horizontal, equally spaced, parallel lines between the plates with arrows pointing to the right, from the positive (left) plate to the negative (right) plate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Work Out the Field Direction**
You have a positive plate on the left connected to + and a negative plate on the right connected to -. Electric field lines always go from positive to negative, so here they must point horizontally to the right.

Step 2: **Show the Field is Uniform**
Between parallel plates, away from the edges, the field is uniform. That means equal strength everywhere, so you draw straight parallel lines that are equally spaced. Draw at least six of them across the gap, all with right-pointing arrows.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
An $\alpha$-particle travels in a vacuum between the two plates.
The electric field does work on the $\alpha$-particle. The gain in kinetic energy of the $\alpha$-particle is $15\text{ keV}$.
Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

markscheme_points.text: gain in KE $= 15 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{3} = 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times V$ (p.d.across plates) or $F$ ($= W/d$) $= 15 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{3} / 16 \times 10^{-3}$; (hence $V = 7500\text{ V}$ or $F = 1.5 \times 10^{-13}\text{ N}$)

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about the alpha-particle itself - what is its charge in terms of the elementary charge e, and what does a gain of 15 keV actually represent in terms of energy transfer?
Hint 2: Convert the energy gain into joules and the plate separation of 16 mm into metres so all quantities are in SI units before you calculate.
Hint 3: Link the kinetic energy gained to the work done by the field, which equals charge times the potential difference across the full 16 mm gap.
Hint 4: Once you have the potential difference between the plates, use the uniform-field relation connecting field strength, potential difference and separation to find E.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Out the Charge and the Energy**
An $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus, so it carries charge $+2e$ where $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. So $$Q = 2e = 3.2 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$$ The gain in kinetic energy is $15 \text{ keV}$. Convert to joules: $$\Delta KE = 15 \times 10^{3} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 2.4 \times 10^{-15} \text{ J}$$ This energy came entirely from work done by the electric field.

Step 2: **Find the Potential Difference Across the Plates**
When a charge $Q$ moves through a potential difference $V$, the work done is $$W = QV$$ Here $W = \Delta KE$, and the particle crosses the whole gap, so $V$ is the p.d. between the plates: $$QV = \Delta KE$$ $$V = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{-15}}{3.2 \times 10^{-19}} = 7500 \text{ V}$$ A common slip is to use $1e$ instead of $2e$ for the alpha-particle. That would double your $V$.

Step 3: **Convert Separation to Metres and Use E = V/d**
For a uniform field: $$E = \frac{V}{d}$$ with $d = 16 \text{ mm} = 16 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 0.016 \text{ m}$. So $$E = \frac{7500}{16 \times 10^{-3}}$$

Step 4: **Calculate E**
$$E = 468750 \text{ V m}^{-1} \approx 4.7 \times 10^{5} \text{ V m}^{-1}$$ This is the uniform field strength between the plates, acting to the right.
